sections.title: One Architectural Improvement Before Sales Orders
paragraphs: While designing Quotation, I noticed another pattern that I think will make KoreVity significantly cleaner.

Rather than giving every transaction its own independent line-item structure (Quotation Line, Sales Order Line, Invoice Line, Purchase Order Line, etc.) with duplicated concepts, we should design a shared Transaction Line architecture.
Each transaction can have its own specialized line entity, but they should all inherit the same conceptual structure:
That gives us consistency across Sales, Purchasing, Manufacturing, and even Service, while still allowing each transaction type to add fields unique to its workflow.
I think this will make both the database model and the application code much more maintainable as KoreVity grows.
Now we reach the first entity that touches the physical world.
The Sales Order is a promise.
The Delivery (Shipment/Fulfillment) is the execution of that promise.
This is where inventory actually leaves the warehouse.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Payment.
Because it completes the entire Order-to-Cash cycle before we switch domains into Procurement.
Finishing one business process completely before starting another will make the architecture much easier to validate, test, and reason about, and it keeps the dependencies flowing in one direction.

Everything we've built so far has been leading to this point.

sections.title: 🎉 Order-to-Cash Complete
paragraphs: Every stage has exactly one responsibility.

sections.title: 🏗️ A Major Milestone
paragraphs: We've now completed the entire Order-to-Cash (O2C) domain.

Combined with the Core Business Foundation, KoreVity can now model the complete customer revenue lifecycle—from the first commercial offer to the final payment—without violating separation of concerns.
This is a significant milestone because every future module (Procurement, Manufacturing, Service, Finance, CRM) will integrate with this workflow rather than replacing it.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next phase should be Procure-to-Pay (P2P), beginning with Purchase Requisition.
Why start there instead of Purchase Orders?
Because organizations don't usually buy things immediately.
The business first identifies a need.
That need becomes a Purchase Requisition.
Only after review and approval does it become a Purchase Order.
Designing the process from the beginning rather than the middle will give KoreVity a cleaner and more complete procurement architecture.
Now we begin the second major business engine.
If Order-to-Cash is about generating revenue,
Architecturally, it should mirror O2C wherever possible.
That consistency is one of the biggest strengths we can build into KoreVity.

sections.title: Phase 3 — Procure-to-Pay (P2P)

Notice how closely it mirrors Sales.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Purchase Requisition is not a Purchase Order.
A Purchase Order is a commitment to a supplier.
A Purchase Requisition is an internal request asking permission to buy something.

sections.title: A Purchase Requisition is an internal request created by a person, department, or business process seeking approval to procure products or services.

sections.title: Responsibilities

paragraphs: With Purchase Requisition complete, a reusable enterprise workflow has become clear:

Projects, HR requests, maintenance requests, travel requests, and capital expenditure requests can all follow the same progression, making KoreVity remarkably consistent for both users and developers.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Purchase Order.
Because it is the procurement equivalent of the Sales Order.
It represents the organization's formal commitment to a supplier and becomes the central operational document for receiving goods, matching supplier invoices, and tracking procurement performance.
Designing it next keeps the Procure-to-Pay lifecycle flowing naturally from intent to commitment.
We're now designing the procurement equivalent of the Sales Order.
These two entities should feel like siblings—not twins.
They solve similar business problems from opposite directions.
That symmetry will make KoreVity much easier to understand.
lists: Sales Order → We promise to sell.
Purchase Order → We promise to buy.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Purchase Order is not a Purchase Requisition.
It is the organization's contractual commitment to a supplier.

sections.title: A Purchase Order is a formal purchasing commitment issued to a supplier specifying products, services, quantities, prices, delivery terms, and commercial conditions.
Purpose
paragraphs: Purchase Order becomes the central document connecting:

sections.title: Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not create supplier invoices.

sections.title: AI Context

sections.title: The Biggest Architectural Decision

sections.title: Supplier Confirmation
paragraphs: Because procurement needs visibility before waiting for deliveries.
This makes KoreVity much stronger than many traditional ERPs.

sections.title: Purchase Order as the Procurement Commitment Engine
Engineering Summary

sections.title: 🏗️ One Important Enhancement
paragraphs: While designing Purchase Orders, I noticed an opportunity to make KoreVity significantly stronger.

sections.title: Procurement Should Support Supplier Collaboration
paragraphs: Instead of treating a Purchase Order as a one-way document, treat it as a collaborative business object.
That doesn't change the Purchase Order entity itself, but it makes it the foundation for a future Supplier Portal.
By designing for that possibility now, we avoid major redesigns later and position KoreVity for enterprise-scale procurement ecosystems.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Goods Receipt.
Because it's the procurement equivalent of the Delivery entity in Sales.
It represents the physical receipt of inventory, updates stock through Stock Movements, validates supplier deliveries, and becomes the basis for supplier invoice matching.
It completes the "commitment → execution" transition in the Procure-to-Pay lifecycle.
Now we reach one of the most important operational entities in the entire ERP.
This entity is where the physical world meets the digital world.
A supplier says they shipped goods.
The Goods Receipt confirms what actually arrived.
This is the procurement equivalent of Delivery—but from the opposite direction.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Goods Receipt is not a Purchase Order.

sections.title: A Goods Receipt is the formal confirmation that products or materials have been physically received, inspected, and accepted into inventory from a supplier.
Purpose
paragraphs: Goods Receipt becomes the operational bridge between:

sections.title: Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own supplier invoices.
It does not own purchasing terms.

sections.title: Receipt Information
paragraphs: Useful for logistics and warehouse operations.

sections.title: Inspection
paragraphs: Enterprise receiving almost always includes quality checks.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Accepted quantity cannot exceed received quantity.
Received quantity cannot exceed remaining ordered quantity (unless explicitly allowed).

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Supplier ABC has delivered incomplete shipments on 14% of purchase orders this quarter."

sections.title: Audit Behavior
paragraphs: Every physical inventory movement remains traceable.

sections.title: The Biggest Architectural Decision
paragraphs: Goods Receipt should update inventory only through Stock Movements.
Exactly the same pattern we established with Delivery.

sections.title: Three-Way Matching Foundation
paragraphs: One of the most important procurement controls in enterprise systems is Three-Way Matching.
A supplier invoice should only be payable when these three documents agree:
If they don't match within defined tolerances, the invoice is flagged for review.
Designing Goods Receipt this way prepares KoreVity for enterprise-grade financial controls.

sections.title: 🏗️ A Major Architectural Milestone
paragraphs: At this point, we now have symmetry between Sales and Procurement.

This isn't just aesthetically pleasing—it creates a consistent mental model for users, simplifies reporting, reduces implementation complexity, and gives AI a predictable process structure to reason about.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Supplier Invoice.
Because once goods are received, the supplier issues an invoice requesting payment.

This is where procurement transitions into Accounts Payable, and it allows us to implement the three-way matching process (Purchase Order ↔ Goods Receipt ↔ Supplier Invoice) before finally completing the Procure-to-Pay cycle with Supplier Payments.
Now we enter one of the most critical financial control points in any ERP.
If implemented correctly, this single entity prevents fraud, duplicate payments, pricing mistakes, and procurement leakage.
This is where Operations hands control to Finance.

sections.title: First Principle

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next and final entity in the Procure-to-Pay cycle should be Supplier Payment.

Completing it will give KoreVity a fully modeled procurement lifecycle, just as we completed the Order-to-Cash lifecycle earlier. At that point, we'll have two complete, end-to-end business processes built on the shared foundation, ready for Finance, Projects, Manufacturing, and Service to integrate with.
This completes the entire Procure-to-Pay (P2P) lifecycle.
Just as Customer Payments completed Order-to-Cash, Supplier Payments complete Procurement.
After this entity, KoreVity will have two complete enterprise business processes designed from end to end.

sections.title: First Principle

A Supplier Payment settles that obligation.

sections.title: A Supplier Payment is a financial transaction that records funds paid by the organization to one or more suppliers in settlement of outstanding financial obligations.

These two processes represent the majority of operational activity in most organizations.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: This is the ideal point to begin Phase 4: Finance Core.
Rather than jumping into Projects or Manufacturing, I recommend we establish the financial backbone first:

Because every completed business process we've built (Sales, Procurement, Inventory) will ultimately post into Finance. Building the accounting foundation next gives every future module a consistent place to record its financial impact, avoiding redesigns later and keeping KoreVity's architecture clean and extensible.
I actually think we've reached one of the biggest architectural milestones in the entire ERP.
Up until now, we've been building business processes.
Now we're about to build the financial truth.
This is where many ERP systems become messy because they mix business documents with accounting. We've deliberately avoided that.
That decision is about to pay off.

sections.title: Phase 4 — Financial Core
paragraphs: The Financial Core should not "run the business."
It should record the financial consequences of what the business does.

sections.title: The Finance Architecture
paragraphs: I recommend we build it in this exact order.
There is no Accounts Receivable module.
There is no Accounts Payable module.
Because we already built those in the business layer.

It is simply the catalog of financial accounts the organization uses.
Think of it as the financial dictionary.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Fiscal Calendar.
Because every accounting transaction must belong to a fiscal year and fiscal period.
Without a fiscal calendar, journals have no authoritative timeline for posting, closing periods, or generating financial statements.
Getting time right before recording money is the cleanest architectural sequence we can follow.
In reality, it controls when money is allowed to exist inside the ERP.
This is the organization's financial clock.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Fiscal Calendar is not a date table.
It is the organization's official accounting timeline.
Business time and accounting time are different.

sections.title: A Fiscal Calendar defines the official accounting years, reporting structure, and financial timeline used by an organization for recording, reporting, and closing financial activity.
Purpose
paragraphs: Fiscal Calendar becomes the foundation for:
Nothing financial exists outside the calendar.

sections.title: Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own journal postings.
It provides the timeline they belong to.

sections.title: Identity
paragraphs: Large organizations may maintain multiple calendars.

sections.title: Fiscal Year Model
paragraphs: This is one of the biggest design choices.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: One active primary calendar per legal entity.

sections.title: AI Context

lists: Which reports belong to which fiscal year?

sections.title: Fiscal Calendar should NOT contain individual periods.
paragraphs: This makes future extensions much cleaner.

sections.title: Support Multiple Calendars
paragraphs: We don't have to expose this complexity immediately, but the architecture should support it from the start.

sections.title: Fiscal Calendar as the Financial Time Engine
paragraphs: Everything financial happens inside this timeline.

sections.title: Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Fiscal Calendar is not a calendar.

sections.title: 🏗️ A Small Refinement to the Architecture
paragraphs: While designing this, I realized one refinement that will make the Finance model even cleaner.
Instead of treating Fiscal Year and Accounting Period as mere data inside the calendar, we should elevate them to full entities.
Each layer has exactly one responsibility:
This follows the same design philosophy we've used throughout KoreVity: small, focused entities connected through clear relationships.
lists: Fiscal Calendar → Defines the accounting system.
Fiscal Year → Defines a reporting year.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Fiscal Year.
It represents a single accounting year within the Fiscal Calendar and becomes the parent of Accounting Periods, year-end closing, annual budgets, and annual financial statements.
Building it before Accounting Period keeps the financial time hierarchy complete and logically consistent.
We're now building the time hierarchy of the accounting system.
We already created the clock (Fiscal Calendar).
Now we define the years that exist on that clock.
This seems simple, but it's one of the most important entities in Finance because every budget, financial statement, closing process, audit, and tax return belongs to a Fiscal Year.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Fiscal Year is not a collection of dates.
It is an accounting period of record.
The Fiscal Year belongs to a Fiscal Calendar.

sections.title: A Fiscal Year represents a complete accounting year within a Fiscal Calendar and serves as the primary reporting, budgeting, and financial closing boundary for an organization.
Purpose
paragraphs: Fiscal Year becomes the parent for:

sections.title: Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own individual journal entries.

sections.title: Relationships

sections.title: Status

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Only one Open Fiscal Year per Calendar (configurable if organizations allow multiple).

Year-End Closing as Its Own Entity

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Accounting Period.
Because it is the actual posting window for accounting.
Journal Entries should never belong directly to a Fiscal Year—they belong to an Accounting Period.
This allows month-end closes, quarterly reporting, reopening specific periods, and precise financial controls without affecting the entire fiscal year.
Now we arrive at what accountants work with every single day.

sections.title: An Accounting Period represents a controlled financial posting window within a Fiscal Year that determines when financial transactions may be recorded, adjusted, and reported.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Journal Entry.
This is the single most important financial transaction in the ERP.

Every business event we've built so far—Sales Invoices, Customer Payments, Supplier Invoices, Supplier Payments, Inventory Movements, Asset Depreciation, Payroll, Projects—will eventually become Journal Entries.
Everything we've designed over the past phases has been leading to this point.
This is the heart of the Financial Core.
"What is the single most important transaction in an ERP?"
lists: Journal Entries record its financial impact.

sections.title: Journal Entry.
paragraphs: Everything else we've built eventually leads here.
They all eventually create Journal Entries.
This is the financial truth of the organization.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Journal Entry is not a Sales Invoice.
It is not a Purchase Order.
A Journal Entry records the financial effect of those documents.
The invoice tells the business story.
The journal tells the accounting story.

sections.title: A Journal Entry is the official accounting transaction that records the financial impact of one or more business events using balanced debit and credit postings.
Purpose
paragraphs: Journal Entry becomes the source for:

sections.title: Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own account balances.
Those belong to the General Ledger.

sections.title: Relationships
paragraphs: Every journal belongs to exactly one accounting period.
Never directly to a fiscal year.

sections.title: Source
paragraphs: One of the most important fields.
Every journal should know why it exists.

sections.title: Journal Lines
paragraphs: This is where accounting actually happens.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: This is the most important rule.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "A manual journal for $250,000 was posted outside normal business hours."

sections.title: Business Modules Never Post Directly to the Ledger
Source Traceability
paragraphs: Every journal should permanently know its origin.
This means an auditor can start from the General Ledger and navigate all the way back to the originating business document.
That's a hallmark of enterprise-grade ERP systems.

sections.title: Journal Entry as the Financial Transaction Engine
Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Journal Entry is not an accounting report.
lists: The source of the General Ledger.
The basis of every financial statement.

sections.title: 🏛️ One of the Biggest Architectural Achievements So Far
paragraphs: At this point, KoreVity has a complete separation between business operations and financial accounting.
This is the same architectural principle used by mature enterprise ERP platforms because it keeps the system maintainable, auditable, and adaptable.
lists: Neither needs to know the internal details of the other.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Journal Entry Line.
Although we've mentioned journal lines throughout this design, they deserve to be a first-class entity.
Because the actual debits, credits, Chart of Account references, Cost Centers, Dimensions, tax allocations, and analytical information all live at the line level—not the journal header.
The Journal Entry is the container.

sections.title: Journal Entry Lines are where accounting actually happens.
paragraphs: This is one of those entities that accountants care about more than almost anything else.
The Journal Entry is merely the envelope.
The Journal Entry Lines contain the accounting.
Without Journal Entry Lines, there is no accounting.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Journal Entry Line is not an independent transaction.
It is one component of a balanced accounting entry.
Neither line means anything by itself.
Together they form the accounting transaction.

sections.title: A Journal Entry Line represents an individual debit or credit posting against a specific financial account as part of a balanced Journal Entry.
Purpose
paragraphs: Journal Entry Lines become the foundation for:
Every ledger balance comes from journal lines.

sections.title: Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own posting status.
Those belong to the Journal Entry.

sections.title: Relationships
paragraphs: Every line posts to exactly one account.

sections.title: Source Reference
paragraphs: Every line should know why it exists.
This enables drill-down from the ledger directly to the originating business line.

sections.title: Cost Center
paragraphs: One of the most important fields.
We'll model Cost Center as its own entity later.

sections.title: Relationships
paragraphs: Every ledger posting comes from a line.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Marketing expense increased 34% because of campaign spending recorded across three cost centers."
lists: Which expense accounts receive the most postings?

sections.title: Lines Own Analytics
paragraphs: Many ERP systems place analytics on the journal header.
Impossible if dimensions exist only on the header.

sections.title: All analytical attributes belong on Journal Entry Lines.
Universal Source Traceability
paragraphs: Every Journal Entry Line should retain a permanent relationship back to the exact originating business line.
This means accountants can drill from a financial report all the way back to the original operational transaction without losing context.
It's an incredibly valuable capability for audits and troubleshooting.

sections.title: Journal Entry Line as the Accounting Engine
paragraphs: This is where accounting truly happens.

sections.title: Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Journal Entry Line is not a child table.
lists: The atomic unit of enterprise accounting.

sections.title: 🏗️ A Major Architectural Realization
paragraphs: At this point, we've completed the entire accounting transaction model.
That means the General Ledger will never be manually edited—it becomes a derived financial view built entirely from immutable Journal Entry Lines.
This is a cornerstone of robust accounting systems.
lists: Journal Entry Lines record the individual postings.
The General Ledger will simply summarize those postings.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be General Ledger.
Because we've now built everything required to populate it.

The General Ledger should not be treated as a place where users enter data. It should be a continuously derived record of account balances and movements based entirely on posted Journal Entry Lines, making it the authoritative financial ledger for reporting and analysis.
This is one of the most misunderstood parts of ERP systems.
People often think the General Ledger is where accountants enter accounting.

sections.title: The General Ledger should never be edited.
paragraphs: It should be the consequence of correctly posted Journal Entry Lines.
That single design decision separates modern accounting systems from poor ones.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: The General Ledger is not a transaction.
It is not an accounting document.
It is the accumulated financial history of every account.

sections.title: The General Ledger is the authoritative financial record that accumulates all posted Journal Entry Lines by account, period, and financial dimensions to provide the organization's official accounting balances and transaction history.
Purpose
paragraphs: The General Ledger becomes the source for:
Everything financial ultimately comes from the Ledger.

sections.title: Should the General Ledger be an Entity?
paragraphs: Many ERPs model it as a table.
I think KoreVity should model it as an entity.
Because accountants work with the Ledger.

sections.title: Running Balance
paragraphs: One of the most important fields.

sections.title: Relationships
paragraphs: Ledger becomes the center of Finance.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Ledger entries created only from posted Journal Lines.

sections.title: Permissions
paragraphs: Because editing the ledger should never exist.

sections.title: Search
paragraphs: Ledger inquiry is one of the most-used accounting features.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Operating Expenses increased 18% because IT software subscriptions grew across three business units."
This comes directly from the Ledger.

sections.title: Immutable Ledger
paragraphs: Many older systems allow direct ledger corrections.
I strongly recommend KoreVity never allow that.

sections.title: Ledger Snapshots
paragraphs: Instead of recalculating decades of transactions every time.
The ledger still derives from Journals—but performance improves dramatically.

sections.title: General Ledger as the Financial Truth Engine
Engineering Summary
paragraphs: The General Ledger is not a place to enter accounting.
lists: The financial truth of the organization.

sections.title: 🏛️ A Significant Architectural Insight
paragraphs: We've now completed the core accounting engine.
This means every business module we've built—Sales, Procurement, Inventory, Assets, and every future module—has exactly one path into Finance.
That dramatically reduces complexity and ensures every financial report is generated from a single, authoritative source.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Cost Center.
Because the accounting engine is now complete.
The next step is enriching it with management accounting.
Cost Centers allow organizations to answer questions like:
In other words, the General Ledger tells you what happened.
Cost Centers begin to tell you where it happened.
This is one of the biggest conceptual shifts in ERP.

sections.title: "Where did it happen, who was responsible, and why?"
paragraphs: That begins with the Cost Center.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Cost Center is not a Chart of Account.

sections.title: A Cost Center is an organizational unit responsible for accumulating, controlling, and reporting costs for operational and management purposes.
Purpose
paragraphs: Cost Centers become the foundation for:

sections.title: Manager
paragraphs: Budgets and approvals usually belong to managers.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Inactive Cost Centers cannot receive new postings.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Marketing exceeded its quarterly budget by 8%, primarily due to digital advertising."
This is management insight, not financial accounting.
lists: Which Cost Center has the highest operating expenses?
Which manager consistently stays within budget?

sections.title: Cost Centers Belong on Journal Entry Lines
paragraphs: Every Journal Entry Line owns its Cost Center.

sections.title: Profit Center
paragraphs: I recommend keeping them as separate future entities.
Trying to merge them creates reporting problems later.

sections.title: Cost Center as the Responsibility Accounting Engine
Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Cost Center is not an accounting account.

sections.title: 🏛️ A Significant Architectural Insight
paragraphs: With Cost Centers in place, KoreVity now supports two independent financial classification axes.
This separation allows the same expense account to be analyzed across multiple departments without duplicating accounts—a hallmark of scalable enterprise accounting.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Financial Dimensions.
Cost Centers answer only one management question: where.
Financial Dimensions allow us to answer many others simultaneously:

By designing Financial Dimensions as a flexible framework rather than hardcoding dozens of fields into Journal Entry Lines, KoreVity gains enterprise-level analytical power while remaining adaptable to different industries and organizational structures.
This is one of the architectural decisions that will determine whether KoreVity remains flexible for the next 20 years.
Eventually every financial table has 30 nullable columns.
We're not going to do that.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Financial Dimension is not a Cost Center.
A Cost Center is one specific type of analysis.
A Financial Dimension is the framework that allows unlimited analysis.
Cost Center is simply a specialized dimension.

sections.title: A Financial Dimension is a configurable analytical classification that allows financial transactions to be categorized across multiple business perspectives without changing the Chart of Accounts.
paragraphs: Without changing the Chart of Accounts.

sections.title: Purpose
paragraphs: Financial Dimensions become the foundation for:

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Inactive dimensions unavailable for new journals.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: Which project generated the highest gross margin?

sections.title: Dimension Assignments
paragraphs: Instead of putting dimensions directly inside Journal Entry Lines.
This is how enterprise financial systems achieve extensibility.

sections.title: Financial Dimensions as the Analytical Engine
Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Financial Dimension is not another accounting field.

sections.title: 🏗️ A Major Architectural Evolution
paragraphs: With Financial Dimensions, KoreVity moves beyond traditional accounting into multi-dimensional enterprise analytics.
All from the same Journal Entry Line, without adding new columns every time the business evolves.
This is one of the key characteristics of mature enterprise platforms—it allows organizations to invent new reporting perspectives without redesigning the database.

sections.title: One Refinement I'd Make
paragraphs: After working through this, I'd slightly refine the model.
Rather than thinking of Cost Center and Financial Dimensions as separate mechanisms, I'd make Cost Center a first-class specialized dimension.

Cost Centers remain a dedicated entity because of budgeting, ownership, and responsibility accounting, but under the hood they participate in the same analytical framework. That gives us the best of both worlds: enterprise flexibility without losing the rich business semantics that Cost Centers deserve.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Budget.
we can finally answer the next management question:

sections.title: "Was this expected?"
paragraphs: Budgets introduce planning, forecasting, variance analysis, and performance management—the next major capability of the Financial Core.
Now we begin managing the future.
This is where Finance changes from:

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Budget is not an accounting transaction.
It never posts to the General Ledger.
It is a financial plan against which actual performance is measured.
The budget doesn't change the ledger.
It gives meaning to the ledger.

sections.title: A Budget is an approved financial plan that defines expected revenues, expenses, assets, liabilities, or other financial targets for a defined period and organizational scope.
Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own actual spending.
Actuals come from the General Ledger.

sections.title: Version
paragraphs: One of the most important fields.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "At the current spending rate, Marketing is projected to exceed its annual budget by 9.4%."

sections.title: Engineering Summary
lists: The planning engine of the ERP.

sections.title: 🏛️ A Major Architectural Achievement
paragraphs: At this point, KoreVity now supports the complete financial management lifecycle.
That's the complete management accounting loop.

sections.title: One Refinement I'd Make
paragraphs: After designing this, I'd introduce one additional entity later:
Instead of only versioning budgets, scenarios let executives compare multiple planning strategies side by side without confusing revisions with alternative futures.
This is a feature commonly found in sophisticated enterprise planning systems and fits naturally on top of the Budget model we've designed.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Financial Statement.
We've now built everything required to produce them:
Financial Statements are not data entry screens—they are derived views of the accounting engine.
They complete the Finance Core by transforming accounting data into information that executives, auditors, investors, regulators, and managers actually consume.
This is the final entity of the Financial Core.
Everything we've built—from the Chart of Accounts to the General Ledger—has been leading here.
Auditors don't start with Journal Lines.
Investors don't ask for the General Ledger.
This is where raw accounting becomes business intelligence.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Financial Statement is not a stored accounting document.
It is a derived financial presentation built from the General Ledger.
The statement never owns accounting data.

sections.title: A Financial Statement is a generated financial report that summarizes General Ledger balances according to a defined reporting structure, accounting period, and reporting standard.
Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own financial balances.

sections.title: Supported Statements
paragraphs: The framework should support multiple statement types.
Do not hardcode only three reports.

sections.title: Relationships
paragraphs: Every report belongs to a reporting period.

sections.title: Report Structure
paragraphs: The statement should not define rows.
Changing account mappings automatically changes reports.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Operating margin decreased from 21.3% to 18.9%, primarily because payroll expenses increased faster than revenue."

sections.title: Financial Statements as the Executive Layer
Engineering Summary
lists: The final output of the Financial Core.

sections.title: 🏛️ What We've Actually Built
paragraphs: Looking at the architecture as a whole, we've created a complete enterprise finance engine.
This is a clean separation of concerns:
Every layer has a single responsibility.

sections.title: One Architectural Refinement
paragraphs: Now that the Financial Core is complete, I'd introduce one more future concept—not as part of this phase, but as an enhancement:

Instead of every statement containing its own layout logic, a reusable reporting framework could define row mappings, calculations, subtotals, KPIs, and presentation rules. That would allow organizations to build entirely custom financial reports without changing code.
